st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: The source supports continuous learning through broader expert participation, meaningful engagement with AI-driven change and sharing practical use experiences. kp.k: Everyday AI experimentation supports shared learning
kp.d: Jen Leonard presents the recurring AI Aha! segment as a way to learn collectively by sharing interesting personal uses of AI. The examples in this episode concern everyday activities rather than legal work; they do not establish changes to legal tasks or professional structures.
qs: And if you're new to the podcast, you will learn that one of the segments is what we call AI Aha!—things that we have used AI to do in our lives that we find particularly interesting. And we think it's helpful to share uses with other people so that we can all learn together.

kp.k: Photo-based AI identification informs a personal health-risk inquiry
kp.d: Bridget McCormack reports photographing a tick through a plastic bag and asking ChatGPT to identify it and explain its relevance to Lyme disease. She says it was a deer tick associated with that concern and recommends carrying ChatGPT and collection bags in the woods. This is a personal anecdote; the transcript reports no independent verification or measured identification accuracy.
qs: And we had a plastic bag, so we put the tick in the plastic bag, and I took a photo of it through the plastic bag and asked ChatGPT to identify the tick and tell me anything I needed to know about whether it was the kind of tick we should worry about with respect to Lyme disease.
And in fact, it was a deer tick, and it was exactly the kind of tick that you had to worry about with Lyme disease.

And I don't know if everybody else is carrying plastic bags for collecting ticks, but I highly recommend having your ChatGPT on you and a few little sandwich bags in your pocket if you're in the woods—because there's a lot to learn with these easy tools.

kp.k: Conversational AI provides motivation, with uncertain long-term effectiveness
kp.d: Leonard reports asking ChatGPT voice mode to persuade her to run when she lacked motivation. She subsequently ran seven miles rather than the intended three, while acknowledging that listening to AI podcasts once outside probably contributed to the longer distance. Her account supports a reported instance of motivational assistance, not a controlled finding about persuasion, and she explicitly questions whether it would work long term.
qs: So I turned on voice mode and said, “I really don't feel like going for a run today. Can you use your powers of persuasion, which I've read about, to convince me to go for a run?”
And it worked. Like, long story short, I went for a seven-mile run when I really had intended to go for a three-mile run. And I was really leaning toward going for no run at all.
I don't know whether that would work long term, but I really enjoyed having somebody there to just, like, tell me to go out and go for a run.
Oh no, I was listening to “AI” podcasts once I got out the door. And that's probably why I ran so long.

kp.k: Follow-up AI encouragement includes rest and alternative exercise
kp.d: Leonard reports returning the next day for encouragement and receiving suggestions to rest, cross-train or undertake strength training rather than necessarily complete another full run. She says she followed the cross-training suggestion and relates the exchange to her concern about injury from increasing mileage too quickly. Both hosts regard the advice positively, but the account provides no clinical assessment or longer-term outcome.
qs: But I did go back the next day and asked it to encourage me again.
And it was interesting because upping your mileage too quickly is a recipe for getting hurt, which is why I had to decrease my mileage in the first place.
And then it encouraged me to do some cross-training, which I did.
It was like, “If you want to go for a run, go for it. But you also might want to take a rest today or build in some strength training.”

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The episode offers no concrete claim about changes to legal services or markets. Its substantive AI claims concern personal uses: tick identification and exercise motivation.
pts.d: Jen Leonard broadly describes AI as reshaping the legal profession but specifies no mechanism, outcome or prediction. In the non-work anecdotes, Bridget McCormack reports using ChatGPT to identify a photographed tick and obtain information about Lyme disease risk. Leonard reports that ChatGPT voice mode persuaded her to go running and, on a subsequent day, suggested rest or cross-training rather than another full run. These are accounts of individual experiences, not predictions of legal-sector transformation.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of the speakers' first-person anecdotes; no legal-sector data, benchmarks or studies are supplied.
pts.d: McCormack recounts one photographed-tick interaction without describing independent confirmation of the identification or risk information. Leonard recounts her behavior after two exercise-related interactions and reads portions of the motivational output. Her reference to having read about AI persuasion supplies no identifiable study or quantitative evidence. She also notes that listening to AI podcasts probably contributed to the length of her run, qualifying attribution of the seven-mile distance to ChatGPT alone. The broad statement about AI reshaping law is not supported with concrete examples in this episode.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The reported effects are immediate and recent; Leonard explicitly leaves long-term motivational effectiveness uncertain.
pts.d: In this 2025 episode, both anecdotes concern recent use, described as occurring the previous week. McCormack's use involved photographing a tick through a plastic bag. Leonard used voice mode and repeatedly requested additional encouragement, then returned the next day. The subsequent rest and cross-training suggestions occurred in the context of her concern about increasing mileage too quickly. No timeframe for legal-sector change is specified.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The concrete beneficiaries described are individual consumer users, not legal-service providers or clients.
pts.d: McCormack presents ChatGPT as an accessible informational aid for people encountering ticks outdoors. Leonard describes personal assistance with exercise motivation and training choices. Although the podcast targets lawyers and legal professionals, the episode does not connect these experiences to their professional work or specify effects on law firms, legal departments, staffing, pricing, clients or access to justice.
